subtitle.en: Greetings, introductions, saying how you are

title.en: “To be” has no word in the present

body.en: Uzbek has no separate word for “am / is / are” in the present. Instead, a personal ending is glued to the word: Men amerikalik-MAN = I am American. The endings are -man (I), -san (you), nothing (he/she), -miz (we), -siz (you, formal or plural), -lar (they).

title.en: Two kinds of “you”: sen and siz

body.en: English has one “you”, Uzbek has two. Sen is for friends, family and children. Siz is the polite form for one person (an elder, a stranger, a teacher) and also the plural “you all”. With siz the verb takes -siz: Qalaysiz? instead of Qalaysan? In this course the polite form is marked in English with “sir”, “ma'am” or “(formal)”, and the plural with “you all” or “(plural)”.

title.en: Word order: the verb comes last

body.en: An Uzbek sentence almost always ends with the verb: subject, then everything else, then the verb. Men Nyu-Yorkda yashayman is literally “I in New York live”. Little words like “in”, “to” and “from” are endings on the noun: Nyu-York-da = in New York.

subtitle.en: Talking about your family and describing people
subtitle.tx: Oila haqida gapirish va odamlarni tasvirlash

body.en: Uzbek says “my mother” in one word: ona + -m = onam. The endings are -(i)m (my), -(i)ng (your), -(s)i (his/her), -(i)miz (our), -(i)ngiz (your, formal or plural). The pronoun can be added for emphasis: mening onam, sening otang, uning uyi.
The Uzbek plural is always -lar, with no exceptions: kitob → kitoblar, do'st → do'stlar. After a number, though, the noun stays singular: uch kitob (literally “three book”).

For a yes/no question add -mi; there is no change in word order. With nouns it comes before the personal ending (Sen o'zbeksan → O'zbek-mi-san?), with verbs after it (gapirasan-mi?). Question words stay where the answer would go: kim (who), nima (what), qayer (where), qachon (when), nega (why).

subtitle.en: Counting, telling the time and talking about the calendar

body.en: Uzbek numbers are completely regular: 11 = o'n bir (ten-one), 21 = yigirma bir (twenty-one). The tens: o'n (10), yigirma (20), o'ttiz (30), qirq (40), ellik (50), oltmish (60), yetmish (70), sakson (80), to'qson (90), yuz (100). When you count things, -ta is often added: uchta kitob (three books).

Time is told with soat (hour, clock): Soat uch = It's three o'clock. “Half past” is yarim after the hour: uch yarim = half past three. Minutes past the hour use -dan ... o'tdi: uchdan o'n daqiqa o'tdi = ten past three (literally “ten minutes have passed from three”).
The ending -da covers English “in”, “at” and “on”, for both place and time: uyda (at home), soat beshda (at five), dushanbada (on Monday).

subtitle.en: Ordering, buying food, talking about tastes

title.en: Bor and yo'q: there is, there isn't

body.en: To say “there is” or “I have”, Uzbek puts bor (there is) or yo'q (there isn't) at the end of the sentence. “I have” is literally “at me there is”: Menda pul bor = I have money. Suv yo'q = There is no water. Add -mi for a question: Non bormi?
When the object is a specific, known thing it takes -ni, which often matches English “the”: Men nonni yeyman = I eat the bread. When it is general, it takes no ending: Men non yeyman = I eat bread.

Uzbek turns “I like” around: the thing you like is the subject, and the person takes the ending -ga (to). Menga choy yoqadi is literally “tea is pleasing to me”. Senga yoqadi = you like it, unga yoqadi = he/she likes it. The negative is yoqmaydi.

subtitle.en: Describing where you live and what's in your home

body.en: Three endings do the work of English prepositions: -da (in, at: uyda = at home), -ga (to: uyga = to the house), -dan (from: uydan = from home). For “on”, “under” or “next to”, Uzbek adds a place word after the noun: stol ustida = on the table (literally “at the table's top”).

title.en: Adjectives come first and never change

body.en: As in English, the adjective comes before the noun, and it never changes: katta uy (a big house), katta uylar (big houses). Only the noun takes the plural ending.

subtitle.en: Asking for directions, getting around, shopping

body.en: The informal imperative is just the bare verb stem: bormoq → bor! (go!), kelmoq → kel! (come!). For the polite form, used with strangers and elders, add -ing: boring, keling. Iltimos (please) softens it further. For “don't”, add -ma: borma! (don't go!).
The standard question is ...ga qanday boraman? = how do I get to…? (literally “how do I go to…?”). “Where is…?” is ... qayerda?: Bekat qayerda? Starting with Kechirasiz (excuse me) is polite.

body.en: The everyday present (also used for habits and the future) is stem + -a- + personal ending: bor-a-man (I go), bor-a-san (you go), bor-a-di (he/she goes), bor-a-miz (we go), bor-a-siz (you go, formal or plural), bor-a-di(lar) (they go). If the stem ends in a vowel, -y- is used instead of -a-: ishla-y-man (I work).
For an action happening right now, like English “am ...-ing”, use -yap- + personal ending: ishla-yap-man (I am working), qil-yap-san (you are doing).
A verb becomes negative with -ma- right after the stem: bor-ma-y-man (I don't go), bil-ma-y-man (I don't know). For nouns and adjectives use emas (“is not”): Men talaba emasman = I am not a student.

title.en: Want to, may I, have to

body.en: Want to: stem + -moqchi + ending (bormoqchiman = I want to go). Can: stem + -a/-y + ola- (bora olaman = I can go, bora olmayman = I can't go). May I: conditional + bo'ladimi (kelsam bo'ladimi? = may I come?). Have to: the verb noun in -(i)sh + possessive + kerak (borishim kerak = I have to go).

Uzbek uses the same tense for the present and the future: Ertaga boraman = I'm going tomorrow / I will go tomorrow. A time word like ertaga (tomorrow) or kelasi hafta (next week) makes the meaning clear.
